passage:
"Another hospital morning," sighed Swati, Karthik's amma, putting down the bag.
"He was so brave with the nurse," said Papa.
Two-year-old Karthik tugged Swati's dupatta. "Bubba!"
"Bubbles? Yes, baby."
They blew bubbles on the balcony. Karthik squealed and chased them.
Then he threw a toy car at the plant.
"No throwing, Karthik," Swati said gently. "Cars drive."
He pouted, then rolled it along the floor, making a vroom sound.
"Hospital days and play days," Papa said, smiling.

qa.q: What did they blow on the balcony?
qa.a: They blew bubbles on the balcony.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel while chasing the bubbles?
qa.a: He felt happy and excited, squealing as he chased them.

qa.q: What did Swati get right after the toy was thrown?
qa.a: Swati kept a normal, gentle rule, no throwing, instead of letting it pass because it was a hospital day.

qa.q: How do the hospital mornings affect Swati?
qa.a: They tire Swati out, which shows in the sigh, but Swati still makes time for play.

grounding: It shows a toddler whose body needs many hospital visits also getting play, comfort and ordinary rules.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday

Tanuja came back today after her week of hospital appointments. She clung to Mummy at drop-off, so I held her on my lap until she was ready. She wears her leg braces now and needed help in the sandpit, but she dug and laughed with the others. At tidy-up she put the blocks away like everyone else. I told Mummy at pick-up that Tanuja had a good day.

Sarita

qa.q: What did Tanuja do at tidy-up?
qa.a: She put the blocks away like everyone else.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling at drop-off?
qa.a: She was unsure and wanted comfort, so she clung to Mummy.

qa.q: Which of Sarita's choices helped Tanuja most?
qa.a: Holding her until she was ready, then helping in the sandpit and asking her to tidy up like the others gave comfort, play and normal expectations.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel hearing the pick-up report?
qa.a: Mummy is likely relieved and happy that Tanuja had a good day after a hard week.

grounding: It shows a toddler with a body that needs extra care getting comfort, play and normal expectations at daycare.

passage: Varun, not yet three, has a heart condition, and some weeks are full of hospital visits. In the waiting room in Hyderabad, Salma always brings his red toy car and lets him zoom it along the benches. At home, though, she treats him like any toddler. He splashes in the sandpit, puts his blocks back in the basket when asked, and gets a firm 'no' when he throws food. Today, after a check-up, he stamped in puddles on the way home, shrieking, and Salma laughed and stamped with him.

qa.q: What does Salma bring to the waiting room?
qa.a: His red toy car.

qa.q: How did Varun seem to feel stamping in puddles?
qa.a: He seemed happy and excited, shrieking with fun after the check-up.

qa.q: What does Salma get right in caring for Varun?
qa.a: She combines medical visits with play, comfort and the same normal rules any toddler has.

qa.q: How might Salma feel stamping in puddles with Varun?
qa.a: She probably feels joyful and relieved to share a normal, playful moment after the hospital.

grounding: Shows a toddler with a long-term condition who needs many appointments, and a parent giving play, comfort and normal expectations alongside medical care.

passage:
'Good morning, Kalyani! Physio first, then park.'
Kalyani, two, kicked her legs.
'Leg braces on. Lift… that's it.'
Kalyani grabbed the Velcro strap. 'Me do!'
'You want to do it? Okay, pull.' Sarika waited while the little fingers tugged. It took ages. 'You did it!'
Kalyani beamed.
'Now shoes. And blocks back in the box before we go.'
'No!'
'Yes. Blocks in the box, then swings.'
Kalyani dropped three blocks in, grinning. At the park Sarika pushed her on the swing, higher and higher, while Kalyani squealed.

qa.q: What did Kalyani grab on the brace?
qa.a: The Velcro strap.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel after doing the strap herself?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, beaming at her mother.

qa.q: What does Sarika do that supports Kalyani well?
qa.a: She lets Kalyani try things herself, keeps normal rules like tidying blocks, and makes time for play after physio.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel waiting while the strap took ages?
qa.a: She may feel a little impatient but glad to let Kalyani be independent.

grounding: Shows a toddler with a long-term condition needing braces and physio, and a parent offering play, patience and normal expectations alongside medical care.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday
Vidya, two, wears two hearing aids and had an audiology appointment this morning, so she arrived after snack. She was clingy at first and wanted cuddles, which we gave. Then she joined the music circle. I sat facing her so she could see my face when I sang, and she clapped along to the drum. At tidy-up time I asked her to put the dolls away like everyone else, and she did it proudly. She laughed a lot at water play.
Lakshmi, room carer

qa.q: Where did Vidya go this morning?
qa.a: To an audiology appointment.

qa.q: How did Vidya seem to feel when she arrived?
qa.a: She seemed clingy and unsettled, wanting cuddles after the appointment.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that included Vidya well?
qa.a: Lakshmi gave comfort first, sat facing her during songs, and kept the same tidy-up expectations as for everyone.

qa.q: How might Vidya's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured that she was comforted, included and treated like the other children.

grounding: Shows a toddler with a long-term condition who has appointments and needs extra care, and a carer offering comfort, play and normal expectations.

passage: In their village near Margao, two-year-old Maria has a brace on her left leg and a hospital card thicker than her picture book. Every second Tuesday, Nirmala, her mother, takes the early bus with her to the city clinic. But at home Maria is just Maria. She bangs pots, chases the hens on her bottom, and hears a firm "no" when she throws rice. After each clinic day, Nirmala lets her splash in the tub and sings the hen song.

qa.q: How often does Nirmala take Maria to the city clinic?
qa.a: Every second Tuesday, on the early bus.

qa.q: How does Maria seem to feel at home, judging by her play?
qa.a: She seems happy and confident, banging pots and chasing the hens like any toddler.

qa.q: What balance does Nirmala strike between care and ordinary life?
qa.a: She keeps up the clinic visits but also gives Maria play, comfort after hard days and the same rules as any child.

qa.q: What might clinic days be like for Nirmala?
qa.a: They are probably long and tiring, starting with an early bus, which is why the bath and song afterwards matter to both of them.

grounding: Shows a toddler with a long-term condition who needs extra medical care yet also gets play, comfort and normal expectations at home.
